# Kaccānijātaka (Ja 417)

**ID:** Ja 417
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Kaccānijātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** When Kaccāni Made a Death-Offering to Dhamma
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja417
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaccānijātaka* (Ja 417) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection. Set at Jetavana, the Buddha relates the story concerning a devoted son in Sāvatthi who faithfully cared for his mother (*mātiposaka*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The narrative opens with the canonical verse beginning *Odātavatthā suci allakesā*, addressed to Kaccāni as she prepares an offering of sesame-rice by a cemetery [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883].

In the story, an elderly mother named Kaccāni is turned out of her home due to the machinations of her ungrateful daughter-in-law [Ching-mei Shyu 2008; Appleton 2010]. As she prepares a death-offering in a cemetery, the god Sakka—identified here as the Bodhisatta—manifests in the air with divine splendor to comfort and rescue her [Appleton 2010; Cowell 1897; Fausböll 1883]. Sakka softens the hearts of her son and daughter-in-law, reconciling the family and enabling Kaccāni to return home in peace [Cowell 1897]. In modern scholarship, the jātaka is cited as an example of Sakka interceding to protect the righteous and as part of the broader pattern of tales contrasting filial piety with domestic discord caused by wicked wives [Ching-mei Shyu 2008; Appleton 2010].

The Pali text of the jātaka is preserved and commented upon in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, with which DharmaNexus identifies substantial textual overlap [Fausböll 1883; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of this jātaka with Kṣemendra's Tibetan translation of the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155) [DharmaNexus]. Depictions of the story and its title, including spelling variants such as *Kaccāyanagotta* and *Kaccāni*, are also attested among the temple inscriptions and jātaka illustrations of the Pagan period in Burma [Win Than Tun 2002].
